newsitem.title: USA: US says Japan firms dumping supercomputers.
newsitem.headline: US says Japan firms dumping supercomputers.

text.p: The Commerce Department Monday backed allegations by Cray Research Inc. that NEC Corp. and another Japanese firm were dumping supercomputers in the U.S. market.
In a preliminary ruling, the Commerce Department found that NEC and Fujitsu Ltd. had offered supercomputers for sale to U.S. customers at less than fair value.

The finding is subject to a final ruling and a determination by the International Trade Commission, an independent U.S. governement agency, that Cray, which requested the antidumping investigation, was actually injured by the sales.

Cray filed the antidumping case last July after it lost a $35 million contract to NEC to supply a supercomputer system to the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR), a research laboratory funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF). Fujitsu had also bid on the contract.

"The findings announced today by the Commerce Department confirm what we have contended since last July -- namely that the four vector supercomputers offered to the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research by NEC were illegally dumped," Cray Research President Robert Ewald said in a statement.

The department's ruling was based on information supplied by Cray because NEC refused to participate in the investigation. NEC, which has said the allegations were groundless, said the agency ruling had been predetermined.

The company has filed suit against the agency in the U.S. Court of International Trade seeking appointment of an independent official to conduct the investigation. The Court of International Trade sits in New York.

"Months before this investigation was even initiated, Commerce, with the approval of then Secretary (Mickey) Kantor, released an analysis finding our company guilty of dumping in order to keep NEC supercomputers out of the U.S. market," HNSX Supercomputers Vice President Samuel Adams said in a statement. HNSX, based in Littleton, Mass., is a U.S. subsidiary of NEC.

"Clearly, Commerce is not capable of judging the dumping allegations subsequently filed by Cray Research in its antidumping petition in a fair and impartial manner," he added. Cray, located in Eagan, Minn., is a subsidiary of Silicon Graphics Inc.
The case is being closely watched in Japan, where the United States has been pushing the government for years to buy more foreign-made computers and other foreign made products.

The UCAR contract has been put on hold while the companies fight over it at the Commerce Department, International Trade Commission and the Court of International Trade where the trial is set to begin April 7.

In the meantime, the U.S. Customs Service will collect a cash deposit on any supercomputers imported into the United States from NEC, Fujitsu and other Japanese firms. Money collected will be held in escrow pending a final ruling.

For NEC, that means a 454 percent duty on the value of supercomputers exported to the United States. For Fujitsu and any other Japanese exporter of supercomputers the margin was set at 27.17 percent of the value of the merchandise.
Margins reflect the amount below fair value that the export merchandise is sold in the United States, a Commerce Department spokesman said.

If the department upholds its preliminary decision in a final ruling, expected by mid-August, the case will then go to the International Trade Commission for a final decision on whether U.S. industry is being hurt by the alleged dumping. That ruling would likely come in early October.
The International Trade Commission issued a preliminary ruling last year finding reasonable evidence of possible injury.
